subChunks.title: WITH — Named Subqueries
subChunks.hookHtml: Nested subqueries become unreadable fast. WITH (Common Table Expressions) gives each subquery a name — turning a dense tangle into a readable sequence of named steps.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Syntax

WITH above_avg AS (
  SELECT name, xp
  FROM   apprentices
  WHERE  xp > (SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices)
)
SELECT * FROM above_avg ORDER BY xp DESC;

Multiple CTEs

WITH
  avg_xp AS (
    SELECT AVG(xp) AS avg FROM apprentices
  ),
  high_earners AS (
    SELECT a.name, a.xp, m.name AS mentor
    FROM   apprentices AS a
    JOIN   mentors AS m ON a.mentor_id = m.id
    WHERE  a.xp > (SELECT avg FROM avg_xp)
  )
SELECT * FROM high_earners ORDER BY xp DESC;

Each CTE can reference any CTE defined before it in the WITH clause.

CTE vs subquery

  • CTEs are named — code reads like steps in a recipe
  • CTEs can be referenced multiple times in the main query (saving re-computation in some engines)
  • CTEs support recursion (next lesson)
  • In most engines, CTEs are not materialised by default — the optimiser may inline them. PostgreSQL 12+ inlines by default; use WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (...) to force materialisation

storyBeats.text: The query spans four sub-queries, nested three levels deep. Nobody can read it tomorrow.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: WITH turns subqueries into named steps. Read it like prose: 'first compute the average, then find those above it, then join to their mentors.' Each step has a name. Each name can be read without unwrapping the nesting. Complex queries become legible.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Named query

Using a CTE, first compute the average XP of the entire table as avg_xp, then return name and xp for all apprentices above that average, ordered by xp descending.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
WITH avg_xp AS (
  SELECT AVG(xp) AS avg FROM apprentices
)
SELECT a.name, a.xp
FROM   apprentices AS a, avg_xp
WHERE  a.xp > avg_xp.avg
ORDER BY a.xp DESC;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns apprentices above average (Bjorn 2400, Cassia 4800, Elara 7500 with avg≈1563)

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Using two CTEs: (1) compute total XP per rank as rank_totals, (2) find ranks where total XP exceeds 2000 as high_ranks. Return the rank names from high_ranks.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what a CTE is, how it differs from a subquery, and when you would use multiple CTEs in a single query.

questions.prompt: What is a CTE (Common Table Expression)?
options: A named temporary result set defined with WITH, scoped to a single query
A permanent view stored in the database
A table variable available across multiple queries
questions.answer: A named temporary result set defined with WITH, scoped to a single query
questions.explanation: A CTE is defined with WITH cte_name AS (...) and exists only for the duration of the query that follows. It is not stored permanently.

questions.prompt: In a WITH clause with multiple CTEs, can a later CTE reference an earlier one?
options: Yes — each CTE can reference any CTE defined before it in the same WITH clause
Only if both CTEs query the same table
Only in PostgreSQL, not in SQLite
questions.answer: Yes — each CTE can reference any CTE defined before it in the same WITH clause
questions.explanation: CTEs are evaluated sequentially within a WITH clause. A later CTE can SELECT from any earlier one by name, enabling step-by-step query construction.

questions.prompt: What advantage does a CTE have over a repeated subquery?
options: The CTE is named and can be referenced multiple times in the main query without rewriting the subquery logic
CTEs are always faster than subqueries
CTEs support JOINs; subqueries do not
questions.answer: The CTE is named and can be referenced multiple times in the main query without rewriting the subquery logic
questions.explanation: A CTE can be referenced multiple times in the same query by name. Whether the engine materialises it or re-evaluates it each time depends on the engine and version, but the code is cleaner and less error-prone than repeated subquery text.

questions.prompt: When would you explicitly use `WITH cte AS MATERIALIZED (...)`?
options: When the CTE is expensive to compute and referenced multiple times — forcing the engine to compute it once and cache the result
When the CTE contains an ORDER BY clause
When the CTE needs to write to the database
When the CTE references a table with more than 1 million rows
questions.answer: When the CTE is expensive to compute and referenced multiple times — forcing the engine to compute it once and cache the result
questions.explanation: By default, modern engines may inline CTEs and recompute them for each reference. MATERIALIZED forces a single computation and caches the result set. Useful for expensive CTEs referenced multiple times, or to prevent the optimiser from inlining in cases where that causes performance issues.
